claim: In 2021, an estimated 619,000 deaths and 247 million malaria cases were reported globally.
source: In 2021, an estimated 619,000 deaths and 247 million cases were reported (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2022 report

claim: Around 70% of malaria deaths occur in African children under five years of age.
source: Around 70% of deaths are in African children under five years of age and are caused by a single parasite species, Plasmodium falciparum (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2022 report

claim: Plasmodium falciparum causes around 70% of malaria deaths in African children under five years of age.
source: Around 70% of deaths are in African children under five years of age and are caused by a single parasite species, Plasmodium falciparum (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2022 report

claim: Gametocytes are the only parasite stage that can progress the life cycle in the mosquito.
source: Between-host transmission requires the formation of gametocytes from asexual blood stage forms, as gametocytes are the only parasite stage to progress the cycle in the mosquito.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about malaria parasite biology

claim: Commitment to gametocyte formation is epigenetically regulated and occurs via activation of the transcription factor AP2-G.
source: A series of recent studies has demonstrated that commitment to gametocyte formation (i.e. stage conversion) is epigenetically regulated and occurs via activation of the transcription factor, AP2-G that in turn induces transcription of the first set of gametocyte genes (Kafsack et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kafsack et al., 2014 and Sinha et al., 2014

claim: AP2-G activation induces transcription of the first set of gametocyte genes.
source: A series of recent studies has demonstrated that commitment to gametocyte formation (i.e. stage conversion) is epigenetically regulated and occurs via activation of the transcription factor, AP2-G that in turn induces transcription of the first set of gametocyte genes (Kafsack et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kafsack et al., 2014 and Sinha et al., 2014

claim: Parasites that do not convert into gametocytes continue to replicate asexually, contributing to within-host parasite population growth.
source: The parasites that do not convert into gametocytes continue to replicate asexually, contributing to within-host parasite population growth (i.e. parasite burden) and determining P. falciparum infection outcome that ranges from asymptomatic infections to severe complications and death (Marsh and Snow, 1999; Langhorne et al., 2008; White, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marsh and Snow, 1999; Langhorne et al., 2008; White, 2018

claim: P. falciparum infection outcomes range from asymptomatic infections to severe complications and death.
source: The parasites that do not convert into gametocytes continue to replicate asexually, contributing to within-host parasite population growth (i.e. parasite burden) and determining P. falciparum infection outcome that ranges from asymptomatic infections to severe complications and death (Marsh and Snow, 1999; Langhorne et al., 2008; White, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marsh and Snow, 1999; Langhorne et al., 2008; White, 2018

claim: Cytoadhesion of infected erythrocytes to microvascular endothelium reduces the rate of parasite elimination in the spleen.
source: Cytoadhesion of infected erythrocytes (IE) to receptors on microvascular endothelium of deep tissues reduces the rate of parasite elimination in the spleen (Rowe et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2013), thus supporting the within-host expansion of the parasite population (i.e. parasite burden).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rowe et al., 2009 and Turner et al., 2013

claim: Cytoadhesion supports within-host expansion of the parasite population.
source: Cytoadhesion of infected erythrocytes (IE) to receptors on microvascular endothelium of deep tissues reduces the rate of parasite elimination in the spleen (Rowe et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2013), thus supporting the within-host expansion of the parasite population (i.e. parasite burden).
evidence: Logical inference from the cited evidence about reduced splenic clearance

claim: Cytoadhesion reduces the diameter of the vascular lumen, impairing perfusion and contributing to severe malaria pathology.
source: As a side effect of this parasite survival strategy, cytoadhesion reduces the diameter of the vascular lumen, thus impairing perfusion and contributing to severe malaria pathology (Silamut et al., 1999; Taylor et al., 2004; Hanson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Silamut et al., 1999; Taylor et al., 2004; Hanson et al., 2012

claim: PfEMP1, encoded by the var multi-gene family, plays a critical role in pathogenesis through cytoadhesion.
source: P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1), encoded by the var multi-gene family, plays a critical role in both pathogenesis (through cytoadhesion) (Smith et al., 1995; Su et al., 1995) and establishment of chronic infection (through variant switching and immune evasion) (Recker et al., 2004; Scherf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 1995 and Su et al., 1995

claim: PfEMP1 plays a critical role in establishment of chronic infection through variant switching and immune evasion.
source: P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1), encoded by the var multi-gene family, plays a critical role in both pathogenesis (through cytoadhesion) (Smith et al., 1995; Su et al., 1995) and establishment of chronic infection (through variant switching and immune evasion) (Recker et al., 2004; Scherf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Recker et al., 2004 and Scherf et al., 2008

claim: Both var gene transcription and stage conversion are subject to within-host environmental pressures such as immunity, febrile temperature, nutritional stress, and drugs.
source: Both var gene transcription and stage conversion (and hence ap2-g transcription) are subject to within-host environmental pressures such as immunity (Rono et al., 2018), febrile temperature (Oakley et al., 2007; Rawat et al., 2021), nutritional stress (Carter and Miller, 1979), and drugs (Buckling et al., 1999), perhaps via a common epigenetic regulation mechanism (Coleman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations for each environmental pressure

claim: var gene transcription and stage conversion may be regulated via a common epigenetic regulation mechanism.
source: Both var gene transcription and stage conversion (and hence ap2-g transcription) are subject to within-host environmental pressures such as immunity (Rono et al., 2018), febrile temperature (Oakley et al., 2007; Rawat et al., 2021), nutritional stress (Carter and Miller, 1979), and drugs (Buckling et al., 1999), perhaps via a common epigenetic regulation mechanism (Coleman et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to Coleman et al., 2014

claim: Stage conversion can be induced by nutritional depletion such as spent culture media in vitro.
source: For example, in vitro studies revealed that stage conversion can be induced by nutritional depletion such as spent culture media (Carter and Miller, 1979; Williams, 1999) and depletion of Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carter and Miller, 1979 and Williams, 1999

claim: Stage conversion can be induced by depletion of Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) in vitro.
source: For example, in vitro studies revealed that stage conversion can be induced by nutritional depletion such as spent culture media (Carter and Miller, 1979; Williams, 1999) and depletion of Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brancucci et al., 2017

claim: Parasites in low transmission settings invest more in sexual commitment and less in replication compared to high transmission settings.
source: Recent work from Kenya and Sudan provides some evidence that parasites in low relative to high transmission settings invest more in sexual commitment and less in replication and vice versa (Rono et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rono et al., 2018

claim: The parasite can sense and rapidly adapt to its environment in vitro and in vivo.
source: Altogether these studies suggest that the parasite can sense and rapidly adapt to its environment in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Inference drawn from the cited studies discussed in the preceding text

claim: Sirtuins link environmental cues to various cellular processes via metabolic regulation.
source: A family of protein deacetylases called sirtuins is known to link environmental cues to various cellular processes via metabolic regulation (Li, 2013; Bosch-Presegué and Vaquero, 2014; Vasquez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li, 2013; Bosch-Presegué and Vaquero, 2014; Vasquez et al., 2017

claim: Sirtuins control cellular processes through epigenetic control of gene expression and post-translational modification of protein function.
source: They do this through epigenetic control of gene expression (Vasquez et al., 2017) and post-translational modification of protein function (Vasquez et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vasquez et al., 2017 and Zhu et al., 2012

claim: The P. falciparum genome contains two sirtuins (Pfsir2a/b).
source: The P. falciparum genome contains two sirtuins (Pfsir2a/b) which have been linked to the control of var gene transcription (Tonkin et al., 2009; Merrick et al., 2012), and their expression is influenced by febrile temperature (Oakley et al., 2007) and low transmission intensity (Rono et al., 2018; O'Meara et al., 2008; Mogeni et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about P. falciparum genome

claim: Pfsir2a/b have been linked to the control of var gene transcription.
source: The P. falciparum genome contains two sirtuins (Pfsir2a/b) which have been linked to the control of var gene transcription (Tonkin et al., 2009; Merrick et al., 2012), and their expression is influenced by febrile temperature (Oakley et al., 2007) and low transmission intensity (Rono et al., 2018; O'Meara et al., 2008; Mogeni et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tonkin et al., 2009 and Merrick et al., 2012

claim: Pfsir2a/b expression is influenced by febrile temperature.
source: The P. falciparum genome contains two sirtuins (Pfsir2a/b) which have been linked to the control of var gene transcription (Tonkin et al., 2009; Merrick et al., 2012), and their expression is influenced by febrile temperature (Oakley et al., 2007) and low transmission intensity (Rono et al., 2018; O'Meara et al., 2008; Mogeni et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oakley et al., 2007

claim: Pfsir2a/b expression is influenced by low transmission intensity.
source: The P. falciparum genome contains two sirtuins (Pfsir2a/b) which have been linked to the control of var gene transcription (Tonkin et al., 2009; Merrick et al., 2012), and their expression is influenced by febrile temperature (Oakley et al., 2007) and low transmission intensity (Rono et al., 2018; O'Meara et al., 2008; Mogeni et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rono et al., 2018; O'Meara et al., 2008; Mogeni et al., 2016

claim: The study included samples and clinical data collected from 828 children in Kilifi county, Kenya, over 18 years of changing malaria transmission intensity between 1994 and 2014.
source: We analyzed samples and clinical data collected from children in Kilifi county, Kenya, over changing malaria transmission intensity between 1994 and 2014.
evidence: Description of the study design and data collection

claim: The study period encompassed three defined transmission phases: pre-decline (1990–2002), decline (2003–2008), and post-decline (2009–2014).
source: The study period encompassed three defined transmission phases: pre-decline (1990–2002), decline (2003–2008), and post-decline (2009–2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Study design definition with reference to Figure 1A

claim: During the study period, a total of 26,564 malaria admissions were recorded at Kilifi county hospital.
source: During the study period, a total of 26,564 malaria admissions were recorded at Kilifi county hospital (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Data from hospital records shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: The mean patient age at admission increased over time during the study period.
source: While the number of parasite-positive admissions decreased, the mean patient age at admission increased over time (Marsh and Snow, 1999; White, 2018; Njuguna et al., 2019; Figure 1A).
evidence: Observation from the data shown in Figure 1A, supported by citations

claim: 552 admissions were pragmatically selected to ensure adequate sampling of the transmission periods and clinical phenotypes.
source: For our study, 552 of the admissions were pragmatically selected to ensure adequate sampling of the transmission periods and clinical phenotypes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Description of study sampling methodology

claim: 150 patients presented with moderate malaria and 402 with one or a combination of severe malaria syndromes.
source: 150 patients presented with moderate malaria and 402 with one or a combination of the severe malaria syndromes: impaired consciousness (IC), respiratory distress (RD), and severe malaria anemia (SMA) (Marsh et al., 1995; Figure 1D).
evidence: Data from the study cohort shown in Figure 1D

claim: 223 samples from children presenting with mild malaria at outpatient clinics and 53 asymptomatic children from a longitudinal malaria cohort study were added to the study.
source: 223 samples from children presenting with mild malaria at outpatient clinics and 53 asymptomatic children from a longitudinal malaria cohort study were added to cover the full range of the possible outcomes of malaria infection (Figure 1B–E), bringing the total number included in this study to 828 children.
evidence: Description of additional samples added to the study

claim: Total parasite biomass (PfHRP2) but not peripheral parasitemia decreased with declining transmission.
source: Total parasite biomass (PfHRP2) but not peripheral parasitemia decreased with declining transmission (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observation from data analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: The decrease in total parasite biomass was significant in patients presenting with mild malaria at outpatient clinics.
source: This decrease was significant in the patients presenting with mild malaria at outpatient clinics which is a more homogenous clinical subgroup as compared to admissions consisting of a range of clinical phenotypes (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the data with reference to clinical subgroups

claim: ap2-g transcription increased significantly with declining malaria transmission.
source: In line with recent findings (Rono et al., 2018), ap2-g transcription increased significantly with declining malaria transmission (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: Data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2B, consistent with cited literature

claim: ap2-g transcription is highly significantly correlated with transcription levels of the gametocyte marker Pfs16.
source: Further analysis demonstrated that ap2-g transcription is highly significantly correlated with transcription levels of the gametocyte marker Pfs16 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The correlation between ap2-g and Pfs16 validates ap2-g as a proxy for both stage conversion and gametocyte levels.
source: This association validates ap2-g as a proxy for both, stage conversion and gametocyte levels.
evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation data

claim: Pfsir2a transcription followed the same trend as ap2-g across transmission periods.
source: Pfsir2a transcription followed the same trend across transmission periods (Figure 2B, right) and was positively associated with ap2-g transcription (Figure 2D).
evidence: Observation from data shown in Figure 2B and 2D

claim: Pfsir2a transcription was positively associated with ap2-g transcription.
source: Pfsir2a transcription followed the same trend across transmission periods (Figure 2B, right) and was positively associated with ap2-g transcription (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical association shown in Figure 2D

claim: Pfsir2a and ap2-g transcription showed a positive association with fever.
source: Pfsir2a and ap2-g transcription also showed a positive association with fever (Figure 2E), suggesting that both factors are sensitive to changes in the host inflammatory response.
evidence: Statistical association shown in Figure 2E

claim: Pfsir2a but not ap2-g transcription showed a significant negative association with PfHRP2.
source: Pfsir2a but not ap2-g transcription also showed a significant negative association with PfHRP2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Pfsir2a transcription showed a positive association with global upregulation of var gene transcription, particularly with subgroup B.
source: Pfsir2a transcription showed a positive association with global upregulation of var gene transcription, particularly with subgroup B (Figure 2F).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: Transcription of group B var subgroup, Pfsir2a, and ap2-g transcription followed a similar pattern in relation to clinical phenotypes.
source: Likewise, transcription of group B var subgroup, Pfsir2a, and ap2-g transcription followed a similar pattern in relation to clinical phenotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Pfs16 expression showed a significant positive correlation with group B and C var genes.
source: Pfs16 expression showed a significant positive correlation with group B (here termed gpb1) and C (gpc2) var genes, while no correlation was observed with the rest of the var subgroups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The markers MCP-1, IL-10, IL-6, and IL-1ra were significantly positively correlated with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription.
source: The markers MCP-1, IL-10, IL-6, and IL-1ra were significantly positively correlated with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Exploratory factor analysis structured the inflammation markers into five profiles with distinct inflammatory states.
source: Factor loadings structured the inflammation markers into five profiles with distinct inflammatory states (Figure 3B).
evidence: Results of factor analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: F1 consists of a mixture of inflammatory markers that support effector Th1/Th2/Th9/Th17 responses (hyperinflammatory state).
source: F1 consists of a mixture of inflammatory markers that support effector Th1/Th2/Th9/Th17 responses (i.e. hyperinflammatory state), F2 represents a Th2 response, F3 represents markers that support follicular helper T cell development and Th17 (Dong, 2021; Chao et al., 2023), F4 represents markers of immune paralysis/tissue-injury linked to response to cellular/tissue injury (Kumar et al., 2014), and F5 represents the inflammasome/Th1 response (Weiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of factor analysis results based on known immunology

claim: F2 represents a Th2 response.
source: F1 consists of a mixture of inflammatory markers that support effector Th1/Th2/Th9/Th17 responses (i.e. hyperinflammatory state), F2 represents a Th2 response, F3 represents markers that support follicular helper T cell development and Th17 (Dong, 2021; Chao et al., 2023), F4 represents markers of immune paralysis/tissue-injury linked to response to cellular/tissue injury (Kumar et al., 2014), and F5 represents the inflammasome/Th1 response (Weiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of factor analysis results based on known immunology

claim: F3 represents markers that support follicular helper T cell development and Th17.
source: F1 consists of a mixture of inflammatory markers that support effector Th1/Th2/Th9/Th17 responses (i.e. hyperinflammatory state), F2 represents a Th2 response, F3 represents markers that support follicular helper T cell development and Th17 (Dong, 2021; Chao et al., 2023), F4 represents markers of immune paralysis/tissue-injury linked to response to cellular/tissue injury (Kumar et al., 2014), and F5 represents the inflammasome/Th1 response (Weiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to Dong, 2021 and Chao et al., 2023

claim: F4 represents markers of immune paralysis/tissue-injury linked to response to cellular/tissue injury.
source: F1 consists of a mixture of inflammatory markers that support effector Th1/Th2/Th9/Th17 responses (i.e. hyperinflammatory state), F2 represents a Th2 response, F3 represents markers that support follicular helper T cell development and Th17 (Dong, 2021; Chao et al., 2023), F4 represents markers of immune paralysis/tissue-injury linked to response to cellular/tissue injury (Kumar et al., 2014), and F5 represents the inflammasome/Th1 response (Weiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2014

claim: F5 represents the inflammasome/Th1 response.
source: F1 consists of a mixture of inflammatory markers that support effector Th1/Th2/Th9/Th17 responses (i.e. hyperinflammatory state), F2 represents a Th2 response, F3 represents markers that support follicular helper T cell development and Th17 (Dong, 2021; Chao et al., 2023), F4 represents markers of immune paralysis/tissue-injury linked to response to cellular/tissue injury (Kumar et al., 2014), and F5 represents the inflammasome/Th1 response (Weiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2018

claim: F4 showed a significant positive association with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription and fever.
source: F4 showed a significant positive association with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription and fever (Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: F5 showed a negative association with ap2-g and fever.
source: In contrast, F5 showed a negative association with ap2-g and fever while F1 was positively associated with fever (Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: F1 was positively associated with fever.
source: In contrast, F5 showed a negative association with ap2-g and fever while F1 was positively associated with fever (Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: F1 and F5 significantly declined with falling transmission.
source: In parallel with the observed decrease in PfHRP2 levels (Figure 2A), F1 and F5 significantly declined with falling transmission (Figure 3D).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The observed negative association between Pfsir2a transcription and PfHRP2 levels appears to be independent of the measured cytokine levels.
source: Of note, the observed negative association between Pfsir2a transcription and PfHRP2 levels appears to be independent of the measured cytokine levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and is hence likely the result of parasite intrinsic regulation of replication.
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The negative association between Pfsir2a transcription and PfHRP2 is likely the result of parasite intrinsic regulation of replication.
source: Of note, the observed negative association between Pfsir2a transcription and PfHRP2 levels appears to be independent of the measured cytokine levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and is hence likely the result of parasite intrinsic regulation of replication.
evidence: Inference from the independence of the association from cytokine levels

claim: Serum phospholipid LPC serves as a substrate for parasite membrane biosynthesis during asexual replication.
source: We have previously demonstrated in vitro that the serum phospholipid LPC serves as a substrate for parasite membrane biosynthesis during asexual replication, and as an environmental factor sensed by the parasite that triggers stage conversion (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to previous in vitro work by the authors, cited as Brancucci et al., 2017

claim: LPC serves as an environmental factor sensed by the parasite that triggers stage conversion.
source: We have previously demonstrated in vitro that the serum phospholipid LPC serves as a substrate for parasite membrane biosynthesis during asexual replication, and as an environmental factor sensed by the parasite that triggers stage conversion (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to previous in vitro work by the authors, cited as Brancucci et al., 2017

claim: Plasma LPC is mainly derived from the turnover of phosphatidylcholine (PC) via phospholipase A2.
source: Plasma LPC is mainly derived from the turnover of phosphatidylcholine (PC) via phospholipase A2, while in the presence of Acyl-CoA the enzyme LPC acyltransferase (LPCAT) can drive the reaction in the other direction (Law et al., 2019; Amunugama et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Law et al., 2019 and Amunugama et al., 2021

claim: In the presence of Acyl-CoA, the enzyme LPC acyltransferase (LPCAT) can drive the reaction from LPC to PC.
source: Plasma LPC is mainly derived from the turnover of phosphatidylcholine (PC) via phospholipase A2, while in the presence of Acyl-CoA the enzyme LPC acyltransferase (LPCAT) can drive the reaction in the other direction (Law et al., 2019; Amunugama et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Law et al., 2019 and Amunugama et al., 2021

claim: LPC is an inflammatory mediator that boosts type 1 immune response to eliminate pathogens.
source: LPC is an inflammatory mediator that boosts type 1 immune response to eliminate pathogens (Huang et al., 1999; Qin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 1999 and Qin et al., 2014

claim: LPC turnover to PC can be triggered by inflammatory responses aimed to repair and restore tissue homeostasis rather than eliminate infection.
source: LPC turnover to PC can be triggered by inflammatory responses aimed to repair and restore tissue homeostasis rather than eliminate infection (Law et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Law et al., 2019

claim: 24 lipid species dominated by phospholipids showed significant association with the inflammatory factors at a false discovery rate below 0.05.
source: 24 lipid species dominated by phospholipids, showed significant association with the inflammatory factors at a false discovery rate below 0.05 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of lipidomics data shown in Figure 4A

claim: F5 showed a significant positive association with one LPC species and negative associations with PC.
source: F5 showed a significant positive association with one LPC species and negative associations with PC, respectively, while F4 showed a significant negative association with three LPC species (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2

claim: F4 showed a significant negative association with three LPC species.
source: F5 showed a significant positive association with one LPC species and negative associations with PC, respectively, while F4 showed a significant negative association with three LPC species (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2

claim: The positive association of LPC with the F5 inflammatory factor is consistent with previous findings that identified LPC as an immunomodulator that can enhance IFN-γ production and the activation of the inflammasome.
source: The positive association of LPC with the F5 inflammatory factor is consistent with previous findings that identified LPC as an immunomodulator that can enhance IFN-γ production and the activation of the inflammasome (Huang et al., 1999; Qin et al., 2014), which results in increased levels of cytokines such as IL-18 (Weiss et al., 2018) and is necessary for eliminating parasites.
evidence: Interpretation of results in context of cited literature

claim: LPC activation of the inflammasome results in increased levels of cytokines such as IL-18.
source: The positive association of LPC with the F5 inflammatory factor is consistent with previous findings that identified LPC as an immunomodulator that can enhance IFN-γ production and the activation of the inflammasome (Huang et al., 1999; Qin et al., 2014), which results in increased levels of cytokines such as IL-18 (Weiss et al., 2018) and is necessary for eliminating parasites.
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2018

claim: Depletion of LPC is associated with elevated markers of tissue injury (F4).
source: Depletion of LPC is also associated with elevated markers of tissue injury (F4), perhaps following uncontrolled parasite growth or maladaptive inflammation.
evidence: Inference from the observed negative association between F4 and LPC

claim: The same pattern of lipid associations with inflammation was observed in a controlled human infection model.
source: Importantly, we observed the same pattern in a controlled human infection model where parasite densities were allowed to rise to microscopic levels, both after sporozoite, and blood-stage infection (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Alkema et al., 2021; Alkema et al., 2022).
evidence: Data from controlled human malaria infection studies shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, supported by citations

claim: LPC species showed a negative association with both ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription levels.
source: Indeed, LPC species showed a negative association with both ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription levels (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C–F

claim: The association between LPC and ap2-g/Pfsir2a was only significant when inflammation is highest (and LPC level lowest), which is at low transmission (post decline).
source: The association was only significant in our data when inflammation is highest (and LPC level lowest), which is at low transmission (i.e. post decline).
evidence: Statistical analysis stratified by transmission period

claim: LPC levels are highest and vary little across patients at high transmission (pre-decline).
source: In contrast, LPC levels are highest and vary little across patients at high transmission (pre-decline).
evidence: Observation from the data analysis

claim: The key relationships described in the study were independently significant in a structural equation model.
source: Importantly, the key relationships described in Figures 2—4 were independently significant in a structural equation model that examined how host immunity modifies the host-parasite interaction, the within-host environment, and parasite investment in transmission or replication (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Results from structural equation modeling analysis in Supplementary file 3

claim: High transmission is associated with a host immune response that promotes parasite killing without compromising the intrinsic replicative ability of the individual parasite.
source: We show that high transmission is associated with a host immune response that promotes parasite killing without compromising the intrinsic replicative ability of the individual parasite.
evidence: Summary inference from the data presented in the Results section

claim: Low transmission is associated with a host immune response that increases within-host stressors (fever, nutrient depletion), which trigger higher parasite investment into transmission.
source: In contrast, low transmission is associated with a host immune response that increases within-host stressors (fever, nutrient depletion), which trigger higher parasite investment into transmission (see also the model in Figure 5).
evidence: Summary inference from the data presented in the Results section, illustrated in Figure 5

claim: The observed associations between the parasite parameters ap2-g, Pfsir2a, and host inflammation remain significant if corrected for transmission.
source: Importantly, the observed associations between the parasite parameters ap2-g, Pfsir2a, and host inflammation remain significant if corrected for transmission, but they are strongest at low transmission (i.e. post decline period) when inflammation and the risk of damaging the host are highest.
evidence: Statistical analysis with transmission correction

claim: The associations between ap2-g, Pfsir2a, and host inflammation are strongest at low transmission when inflammation and the risk of damaging the host are highest.
source: Importantly, the observed associations between the parasite parameters ap2-g, Pfsir2a, and host inflammation remain significant if corrected for transmission, but they are strongest at low transmission (i.e. post decline period) when inflammation and the risk of damaging the host are highest.
evidence: Statistical analysis stratified by transmission period

claim: Inflammation can influence the within-host environment and modulate parasite investment in replication versus reproduction by altering the levels of environmental stressors.
source: At a systemic level, inflammation can influence the within-host environment and modulate parasite investment in replication versus reproduction by altering the levels of environmental stressors (e.g. oxidative, thermal, or nutritional stress).
evidence: Inference from the observed associations in the data

claim: A pro-inflammatory response mediated by IFN-γ/IL-18 (F5) promoting pathogen killing is negatively associated with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that a pro-inflammatory response mediated by IFN-γ/IL-18 (F5 in our analysis) promoting pathogen killing (Weiss et al., 2018; Hoffman et al., 1997; Kearney et al., 2013) is negatively associated with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription.
evidence: Data analysis with interpretation supported by citations

claim: Inflammatory markers that increase within-host environmental stress or reflect the extent of host tissue injury (F4) are positively associated with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription.
source: In contrast, inflammatory markers that increase within-host environmental stress (e.g. fever) or reflect the extent of host tissue injury and are secreted to heal and restore homeostasis rather than kill pathogens (F4) (Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2021) are positively associated with ap2-g and Pfsir2a transcription.
evidence: Data analysis with interpretation supported by citations

claim: LPC levels are negatively associated with ap2-g transcription in patient plasma.
source: Here, we reveal that LPC levels are negatively associated with ap2-g transcription in patient plasma, thus providing direct evidence for our in vitro findings (Brancucci et al., 2017) across a large malaria patient cohort.
evidence: Statistical analysis of lipidomics and qRT-PCR data from patient samples

claim: LPC is an immune effector molecule promoting macrophage polarization to M1 phenotype that induces the secretion of various cytokines such as IFN-γ and IL-1 family.
source: LPC is an immune effector molecule promoting macrophage polarization to M1 phenotype that induces the secretion of various cytokines such as IFN-γ and IL-1 family (i.e. IL-18) (Huang et al., 1999; Qin et al., 2014) through activation of the inflammasome in endothelial cells and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 1999 and Qin et al., 2014

claim: LPC is the main component of the oxidized form of LDL (oxLDL) that induces inflammasome-mediated trained immunity in human monocytes.
source: Furthermore, LPC is the main component of the oxidized form of LDL (oxLDL) that induces inflammasome-mediated trained immunity in human monocytes (Law et al., 2019; Amunugama et al., 2021), resulting in increased responsiveness to LPS re-stimulation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Law et al., 2019 and Amunugama et al., 2021

claim: LPC levels are positively associated with IFN-γ/IL-18 levels (Factor 5).
source: Indeed, we demonstrate that LPC levels are positively associated with IFN-γ/IL-18 levels (Factor 5).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the study data

claim: LPC levels decreased in the acute phase compared to the pre-challenge and the chronic phase in experimentally infected macaques and malaria patients.
source: These observations are in line with recent data from experimentally infected macaques and malaria patients, where LPC levels decreased in the acute phase compared to the pre-challenge and the chronic phase (Cordy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cordy et al., 2019

claim: LPC is a nutritional resource required by the parasite for replication.
source: LPC is also a nutritional resource required by the parasite for replication (Brancucci et al., 2017) and hence scarcity is expected to promote reproduction, as gametocytes require less nutritional resource and, therefore, provide a better adaptation strategy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brancucci et al., 2017

claim: LPC scarcity is expected to promote reproduction, as gametocytes require less nutritional resource.
source: LPC is also a nutritional resource required by the parasite for replication (Brancucci et al., 2017) and hence scarcity is expected to promote reproduction, as gametocytes require less nutritional resource and, therefore, provide a better adaptation strategy.
evidence: Logical inference from the nutritional requirements of different parasite stages

claim: PfSir2a belongs to the evolutionarily conserved family of sirtuins that act as environmental sensors to regulate various cellular processes.
source: PfSir2a belongs to the evolutionarily conserved family of sirtuins that act as environmental sensors to regulate various cellular processes (Li, 2013; Vasquez et al., 2017; Palacios et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li, 2013; Vasquez et al., 2017; Palacios et al., 2009

claim: PfSir2a and PfSir2b paralogues cooperate to regulate virulence gene transcription including var genes.
source: In P. falciparum, PfSir2a and PfSir2b paralogues cooperate to regulate virulence gene transcription including var genes (Tonkin et al., 2009; Duraisingh et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tonkin et al., 2009 and Duraisingh et al., 2005

claim: Increased PfSir2a levels are associated with reduced parasite replication (lower merozoite numbers) in vitro.
source: In vitro data have also demonstrated that increased PfSir2a levels are associated with reduced parasite replication (i.e. lower merozoite numbers) (Mancio-Silva et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mancio-Silva et al., 2013

claim: The upregulation of Pfsir2a transcription in response to inflammation is part of an orchestrated stress response linking replication and antigenic variation to reproduction and transmission.
source: We hypothesize that the observed upregulation of Pfsir2a transcription in response to inflammation is part of an orchestrated stress response linking replication and antigenic variation (via Pfsir2a) to reproduction and transmission (via ap2-g), perhaps through a shared epigenetic control mechanism (Coleman et al., 2014).
evidence: Hypothesis based on the observed data and supported by citation to Coleman et al., 2014

claim: Host tolerance to malaria infection reduces with falling transmission.
source: It is well known that host tolerance to malaria infection reduces with falling transmission (Borrmann et al., 2011; Dollat et al., 2019), as shown by the declining threshold of parasite biomass (PfHRP2) required for clinical malaria.
evidence: Supported by citations to Borrmann et al., 2011 and Dollat et al., 2019

claim: The declining threshold of parasite biomass required for clinical malaria demonstrates that host tolerance reduces with falling transmission.
source: It is well known that host tolerance to malaria infection reduces with falling transmission (Borrmann et al., 2011; Dollat et al., 2019), as shown by the declining threshold of parasite biomass (PfHRP2) required for clinical malaria.
evidence: Inference from the observed data in the study

claim: Parasites have more pronounced harmful consequences on the infected host in low compared to high transmission settings, perhaps due to increasing host age.
source: This suggests that parasites have more pronounced harmful consequences on the infected host (i.e. clinical symptoms) in low compared to high transmission settings, perhaps due to increasing host age (Sorci et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference from the data with speculative explanation supported by citation to Sorci et al., 2021

claim: Parasites experience increased within-host stress in low transmission settings to which they respond through increased ap2-g transcription and increased Pfsir2a transcription as part of a self-preservation strategy.
source: Under this scenario, we propose that parasites experience increased within-host stress to which they respond through increased ap2-g transcription (to increase reproduction, hence transmission) and increased Pfsir2a transcription (to affect stress coping mechanisms at the expense of replication, hence the negative association with PfHRP2) – as part of a self-preservation strategy in the face of imminent risk of host death.
evidence: Proposed model based on integration of all the study findings

claim: Falling host immunity with declining transmission modifies the predominant host immune response and consequently the within-host environment, resulting in increased investment in transmission and limiting replication.
source: In summary, we propose a model where the falling host immunity with declining transmission modifies the predominant host immune response, and consequently, the within-host environment (e.g. LPC availability, fever), resulting in increased investment in transmission (i.e. higher ap2-g transcription) and limiting replication (i.e. higher Pfsir2a transcription).
evidence: Summary model integrating all findings from the study

claim: Parasite populations in elimination scenarios may increase their transmission potential.
source: They suggest that parasite populations in elimination scenarios may increase their transmission potential.
evidence: Inference from the study findings about parasite adaptation

claim: Understanding how malaria parasites adapt to their environment by increasing investment in transmission stages at low endemicity is highly relevant for public health.
source: Understanding how malaria parasites adapt to their environment, for example by increasing investment in transmission stages at low endemicity, is highly relevant for public health.
evidence: Statement about the public health implications of the findings

claim: Increased parasite investment in transmission at low endemicity would affect the timelines for successful elimination.
source: Not only would this affect the timelines for successful elimination, but it would also form an important argument for the deployment of gametocytocidal drugs once transmission has been successfully reduced.
evidence: Inference about public health implications

claim: Increased parasite investment in transmission at low endemicity forms an important argument for the deployment of gametocytocidal drugs once transmission has been successfully reduced.
source: Not only would this affect the timelines for successful elimination, but it would also form an important argument for the deployment of gametocytocidal drugs once transmission has been successfully reduced.
evidence: Inference about public health strategy implications

claim: Inflammatory responses associated with reduced plasma lysophosphatidylcholine levels are associated with markers of increased investment in parasite sexual reproduction and reduced growth.
source: We find that inflammatory responses associated with reduced plasma lysophosphatidylcholine levels are associated with markers of increased investment in parasite sexual reproduction (i.e. transmission investment) and reduced growth (i.e. asexual replication).
evidence: Summary of key findings from the study data

claim: The association between inflammatory responses, reduced LPC, and increased transmission investment becomes stronger with falling transmission.
source: This association becomes stronger with falling transmission and suggests that parasites can rapidly respond to the within-host environment, which in turn is subject to changing transmission.
evidence: Summary of key findings from the study data

claim: Parasites can rapidly respond to the within-host environment, which in turn is subject to changing transmission.
source: This association becomes stronger with falling transmission and suggests that parasites can rapidly respond to the within-host environment, which in turn is subject to changing transmission.
evidence: Inference from the observed associations in the data
